 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q190556#sitelinks-wikipedia)                         [![Listen to this article](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/20px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:En-De_Moivres_Formula-article.ogg)   From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

 Theorem: (cos x + i sin x)^n = cos nx + i sin nxNot to be confused with [De Moivre–Laplace theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre%E2%80%93Laplace_theorem).

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), **de Moivre's formula** (also known as **de Moivre's theorem** and **de Moivre's identity**) states that for any [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) x and [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) n,       (   cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x    )    n   = cos ⁡ n x + i sin ⁡ n x ,   {\displaystyle {\big (}\cos x+i\sin x{\big )}^{n}=\cos nx+i\sin nx,}   where i is the [imaginary unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_unit) (*i*2 = −1). The formula is named after [Abraham de Moivre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_de_Moivre),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre's_formula#cite_note-1) although he never stated it in his works.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre's_formula#cite_note-2) The expression cos *x* + *i* sin *x* is sometimes abbreviated to [cis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cis_(mathematics)) *x*.

The formula is important because it connects [complex numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_numbers) and [trigonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometry). By expanding the left hand side and then comparing the real and imaginary parts under the assumption that x is real, it is possible to derive useful expressions for cos *nx* and sin *nx* in terms of cos *x* and sin *x*.

As written, the formula is not valid for non-integer powers n. However, there are generalizations of this formula valid for other exponents. These can be used to give explicit expressions for the nth [roots of unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_unity), that is, [complex numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_numbers) z such that *zn* = 1.

Using the standard extensions of the sine and cosine functions to complex numbers, the formula is valid even when x is an arbitrary complex number.

## Example

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=1)]

For     x =   π 6     {\displaystyle x={\frac {\pi }{6}}}   and     n = 2   {\displaystyle n=2}  , de Moivre's formula asserts that       (  cos ⁡   (     π 6     )   + i sin ⁡   (     π 6     )    )   2   = cos ⁡   (   2 ⋅   π 6     )   + i sin ⁡   (   2 ⋅   π 6     )   ,   {\displaystyle \left(\cos {\bigg (}{\frac {\pi }{6}}{\bigg )}+i\sin {\bigg (}{\frac {\pi }{6}}{\bigg )}\right)^{2}=\cos {\bigg (}2\cdot {\frac {\pi }{6}}{\bigg )}+i\sin {\bigg (}2\cdot {\frac {\pi }{6}}{\bigg )},}   or equivalently that       (     3  2   +   i 2    )   2   =   1 2   +    i   3    2   .   {\displaystyle \left({\frac {\sqrt {3}}{2}}+{\frac {i}{2}}\right)^{2}={\frac {1}{2}}+{\frac {i{\sqrt {3}}}{2}}.}   In this example, it is easy to check the validity of the equation by multiplying out the left side.

## Relation to Euler's formula

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=2)]

De Moivre's formula is a precursor to [Euler's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler's_formula)      e  i x   = cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x ,   {\displaystyle e^{ix}=\cos x+i\sin x,}   with x expressed in [radians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radian) rather than [degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_(angle)), which establishes the fundamental relationship between the trigonometric functions and the complex exponential function.

One can derive de Moivre's formula using Euler's formula and the [exponential law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiation) for integer powers

       (  e  i x   )   n   =  e  i n x   ,   {\displaystyle \left(e^{ix}\right)^{n}=e^{inx},}

since Euler's formula implies that the left side is equal to       (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   n     {\displaystyle \left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{n}}   while the right side is equal to     cos ⁡ n x + i sin ⁡ n x .   {\displaystyle \cos nx+i\sin nx.}

## Proof by induction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=3)]

The truth of de Moivre's theorem can be established by using mathematical induction for natural numbers, and extended to all integers from there. For an integer n, call the following statement S(*n*):

     ( cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )  n   = cos ⁡ n x + i sin ⁡ n x .   {\displaystyle (\cos x+i\sin x)^{n}=\cos nx+i\sin nx.}

For *n* > 0, we proceed by [mathematical induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction). S(1) is clearly true. For our hypothesis, we assume S(*k*) is true for some natural k. That is, we assume

       (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   k   = cos ⁡ k x + i sin ⁡ k x .   {\displaystyle \left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{k}=\cos kx+i\sin kx.}

Now, considering S(*k* + 1):

           (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   k + 1      =   (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   k    (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )        =  (  cos ⁡ k x + i sin ⁡ k x  )   (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )       via induction hypothesis        = cos ⁡ k x cos ⁡ x − sin ⁡ k x sin ⁡ x + i  (  cos ⁡ k x sin ⁡ x + sin ⁡ k x cos ⁡ x  )        = cos ⁡ ( ( k + 1 ) x ) + i sin ⁡ ( ( k + 1 ) x )      via trigonometric identities        {\displaystyle {\begin{alignedat}{2}\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{k+1}&=\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{k}\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)\\&=\left(\cos kx+i\sin kx\right)\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)&&\qquad {\text{via induction hypothesis}}\\&=\cos kx\cos x-\sin kx\sin x+i\left(\cos kx\sin x+\sin kx\cos x\right)\\&=\cos((k+1)x)+i\sin((k+1)x)&&\qquad {\text{via trigonometric identities}}\end{alignedat}}}

See [angle sum and difference identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_identities#Angle_sum_and_difference_identities).

We deduce that S(*k*) implies S(*k* + 1). By the principle of mathematical induction it follows that the result is true for all natural numbers. Now, S(0) is clearly true since cos(0*x*) + *i* sin(0*x*) = 1 + 0*i* = 1. Finally, for the negative integer cases, we consider an exponent of −*n* for natural n.

           (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   − n      =   (     (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   n      )    − 1         =   (  cos ⁡ n x + i sin ⁡ n x  )   − 1         = cos ⁡ n x − i sin ⁡ n x   ( ∗ )       = cos ⁡ ( − n x ) + i sin ⁡ ( − n x ) .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{-n}&={\big (}\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{n}{\big )}^{-1}\\&=\left(\cos nx+i\sin nx\right)^{-1}\\&=\cos nx-i\sin nx\qquad \qquad (*)\\&=\cos(-nx)+i\sin(-nx).\\\end{aligned}}}

The equation (*) is a result of the identity

      z  − 1   =     z ¯     |  z   |   2      ,   {\displaystyle z^{-1}={\frac {\bar {z}}{|z|^{2}}},}

for *z* = cos *nx* + *i* sin *nx*. Hence, S(*n*) holds for all integers n.

## Formulae for cosine and sine individually

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=4)] See also: [List of trigonometric identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_trigonometric_identities)

For an equality of [complex numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number), one necessarily has equality both of the [real parts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_part) and of the [imaginary parts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_part) of both members of the equation. If x, and therefore also cos *x* and sin *x*, are [real numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number), then the identity of these parts can be written using [binomial coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_coefficient). This formula was given by 16th century French mathematician [François Viète](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Vi%C3%A8te):

         sin ⁡ n x    =  ∑  k = 0   n      (   n k   )    ( cos ⁡ x  )  k    ( sin ⁡ x  )  n − k    sin ⁡    ( n − k ) π  2       cos ⁡ n x    =  ∑  k = 0   n      (   n k   )    ( cos ⁡ x  )  k    ( sin ⁡ x  )  n − k    cos ⁡    ( n − k ) π  2   .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}\sin nx&=\sum _{k=0}^{n}{\binom {n}{k}}(\cos x)^{k}\,(\sin x)^{n-k}\,\sin {\frac {(n-k)\pi }{2}}\\\cos nx&=\sum _{k=0}^{n}{\binom {n}{k}}(\cos x)^{k}\,(\sin x)^{n-k}\,\cos {\frac {(n-k)\pi }{2}}.\end{aligned}}}

In each of these two equations, the final [trigonometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions) equals one or minus one or zero, thus removing half the entries in each of the sums. These equations are in fact valid even for complex values of x, because both sides are [entire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entire_function) (that is, [holomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function) on the whole [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane)) functions of x, and two such functions that coincide on the real axis necessarily coincide everywhere. Here are the concrete instances of these equations for *n* = 2 and *n* = 3:

         cos ⁡ 2 x    =   (  cos ⁡ x  )   2   +  (    (  cos ⁡ x  )   2   − 1  )      =     2   (  cos ⁡ x  )   2   − 1     sin ⁡ 2 x    = 2  (  sin ⁡ x  )   (  cos ⁡ x  )        cos ⁡ 3 x    =   (  cos ⁡ x  )   3   + 3 cos ⁡ x  (    (  cos ⁡ x  )   2   − 1  )      =     4   (  cos ⁡ x  )   3   − 3 cos ⁡ x     sin ⁡ 3 x    = 3   (  cos ⁡ x  )   2    (  sin ⁡ x  )  −   (  sin ⁡ x  )   3       =     3 sin ⁡ x − 4   (  sin ⁡ x  )   3   .       {\displaystyle {\begin{alignedat}{2}\cos 2x&=\left(\cos x\right)^{2}+\left(\left(\cos x\right)^{2}-1\right)&{}={}&2\left(\cos x\right)^{2}-1\\\sin 2x&=2\left(\sin x\right)\left(\cos x\right)&&\\\cos 3x&=\left(\cos x\right)^{3}+3\cos x\left(\left(\cos x\right)^{2}-1\right)&{}={}&4\left(\cos x\right)^{3}-3\cos x\\\sin 3x&=3\left(\cos x\right)^{2}\left(\sin x\right)-\left(\sin x\right)^{3}&{}={}&3\sin x-4\left(\sin x\right)^{3}.\end{alignedat}}}

The right-hand side of the formula for cos *nx* is in fact the value *T**n*(cos *x*) of the [Chebyshev polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_polynomial) *T**n* at cos *x*.

## Failure for non-integer powers, and generalization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=5)]

De Moivre's formula does not hold for non-integer powers. The derivation of de Moivre's formula above involves a complex number raised to the integer power n. If a complex number is raised to a non-integer power, the result is [multiple-valued](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple-valued) (see [failure of power and logarithm identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiation#Failure_of_power_and_logarithm_identities)).

### Roots of complex numbers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=6)]

A modest extension of the version of de Moivre's formula given in this article can be used to find [the n-th roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nth_root) of a complex number for a non-zero integer n. If z is a complex number, written in [polar form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_form) as     z = r  (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )  ,   {\displaystyle z=r\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right),}   then the n-th roots of z are given by      r   1 n     (  cos ⁡    x + 2 π k  n   + i sin ⁡    x + 2 π k  n    )    {\displaystyle r^{\frac {1}{n}}\left(\cos {\frac {x+2\pi k}{n}}+i\sin {\frac {x+2\pi k}{n}}\right)}   where k varies over the integer values from 0 to |*n*| − 1. This formula is also sometimes known as de Moivre's formula.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre's_formula#cite_note-3)

### Complex numbers raised to an arbitrary power

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=7)]

Generally, if     z = r  (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )    {\displaystyle z=r\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)}   (in polar form) and w are arbitrary complex numbers, then the set of possible values is      z  w   =  r  w     (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   w   = {  r  w   cos ⁡ ( x w + 2 π k w ) + i  r  w   sin ⁡ ( x w + 2 π k w )  |  k ∈  Z  }  .   {\displaystyle z^{w}=r^{w}\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{w}=\lbrace r^{w}\cos(xw+2\pi kw)+ir^{w}\sin(xw+2\pi kw)|k\in \mathbb {Z} \rbrace \,.}   (Note that if w is a [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number) that equals *p* / *q* in [lowest terms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowest_terms) then this set will have exactly q distinct values rather than infinitely many. In particular, if w is an integer then the set will have exactly one value, as previously discussed.) In contrast, de Moivre's formula gives      r  w   ( cos ⁡ x w + i sin ⁡ x w )  ,   {\displaystyle r^{w}(\cos xw+i\sin xw)\,,}   which is just the single value from this set corresponding to *k* = 0.

## Analogues in other settings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=8)]

### Hyperbolic trigonometry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=9)]

Since cosh *x* + sinh *x* = *ex*, an analog to de Moivre's formula also applies to the [hyperbolic trigonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_function). For all [integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) n,

 **( cosh ⁡ x + sinh ⁡ x  )  n   = cosh ⁡ n x + sinh ⁡ n x .   {\displaystyle (\cosh x+\sinh x)^{n}=\cosh nx+\sinh nx.}**

If n is a [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number) (but not necessarily an integer), then cosh *nx* + sinh *nx* will be one of the values of (cosh *x* + sinh *x*)*n*.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre's_formula#cite_note-4)

### Extension to complex numbers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=10)]

For any integer n, the formula holds for any complex number     z = x + i y   {\displaystyle z=x+iy}

     ( cos ⁡ z + i sin ⁡ z  )  n   = cos ⁡  n z  + i sin ⁡  n z  .   {\displaystyle (\cos z+i\sin z)^{n}=\cos {nz}+i\sin {nz}.}

where

         cos ⁡ z = cos ⁡ ( x + i y )    = cos ⁡ x cosh ⁡ y − i sin ⁡ x sinh ⁡ y  ,     sin ⁡ z = sin ⁡ ( x + i y )    = sin ⁡ x cosh ⁡ y + i cos ⁡ x sinh ⁡ y  .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}\cos z=\cos(x+iy)&=\cos x\cosh y-i\sin x\sinh y\,,\\\sin z=\sin(x+iy)&=\sin x\cosh y+i\cos x\sinh y\,.\end{aligned}}}

### Quaternions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=11)]

To find the roots of a [quaternion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternion) there is an analogous form of de Moivre's formula. A quaternion in the form

     q = d + a    i ^    + b    j ^    + c    k ^      {\displaystyle q=d+a\mathbf {\hat {i}} +b\mathbf {\hat {j}} +c\mathbf {\hat {k}} }

can be represented in the form

     q = k ( cos ⁡ θ + ε sin ⁡ θ )    for    0 ≤ θ < 2 π .   {\displaystyle q=k(\cos \theta +\varepsilon \sin \theta )\qquad {\mbox{for }}0\leq \theta <2\pi .}

In this representation,

     k =    d  2   +  a  2   +  b  2   +  c  2     ,   {\displaystyle k={\sqrt {d^{2}+a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}},}

and the trigonometric functions are defined as

     cos ⁡ θ =   d k      and    sin ⁡ θ = ±     a  2   +  b  2   +  c  2    k   .   {\displaystyle \cos \theta ={\frac {d}{k}}\quad {\mbox{and}}\quad \sin \theta =\pm {\frac {\sqrt {a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}{k}}.}

In the case that *a*2 + *b*2 + *c*2 ≠ 0,

     ε = ±    a    i ^    + b    j ^    + c    k ^       a  2   +  b  2   +  c  2      ,   {\displaystyle \varepsilon =\pm {\frac {a\mathbf {\hat {i}} +b\mathbf {\hat {j}} +c\mathbf {\hat {k}} }{\sqrt {a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}},}

that is, the [unit vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_vector). This leads to the variation of De Moivre's formula:

      q  n   =  k  n   ( cos ⁡ n θ + ε sin ⁡ n θ ) .   {\displaystyle q^{n}=k^{n}(\cos n\theta +\varepsilon \sin n\theta ).}  [[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre's_formula#cite_note-5)

#### Example

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=12)]

To find the [cube roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cube_root) of

     Q = 1 +    i ^    +    j ^    +    k ^    ,   {\displaystyle Q=1+\mathbf {\hat {i}} +\mathbf {\hat {j}} +\mathbf {\hat {k}} ,}

write the quaternion in the form

     Q = 2  (  cos ⁡   π 3   + ε sin ⁡   π 3    )     where    ε =       i ^    +    j ^    +    k ^      3    .   {\displaystyle Q=2\left(\cos {\frac {\pi }{3}}+\varepsilon \sin {\frac {\pi }{3}}\right)\qquad {\mbox{where }}\varepsilon ={\frac {\mathbf {\hat {i}} +\mathbf {\hat {j}} +\mathbf {\hat {k}} }{\sqrt {3}}}.}

Then the cube roots are given by:

       Q  3    =   2  3    ( cos ⁡ θ + ε sin ⁡ θ )    for    θ =   π 9   ,    7 π  9   ,    13 π  9   .   {\displaystyle {\sqrt[{3}]{Q}}={\sqrt[{3}]{2}}(\cos \theta +\varepsilon \sin \theta )\qquad {\mbox{for }}\theta ={\frac {\pi }{9}},{\frac {7\pi }{9}},{\frac {13\pi }{9}}.}

### 2 × 2 matrices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=13)]

With matrices,        (    cos ⁡ ϕ   − sin ⁡ ϕ     sin ⁡ ϕ   cos ⁡ ϕ    )    n   =   (    cos ⁡ n ϕ   − sin ⁡ n ϕ     sin ⁡ n ϕ   cos ⁡ n ϕ    )     {\displaystyle {\begin{pmatrix}\cos \phi &-\sin \phi \\\sin \phi &\cos \phi \end{pmatrix}}^{n}={\begin{pmatrix}\cos n\phi &-\sin n\phi \\\sin n\phi &\cos n\phi \end{pmatrix}}}   when n is an integer. This is a direct consequence of the [isomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism) between the matrices of type       (    a   − b     b   a    )     {\displaystyle {\begin{pmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{pmatrix}}}   and the [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane).

 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q190556#sitelinks-wikipedia)                         [![Listen to this article](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/20px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:En-De_Moivres_Formula-article.ogg)   From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

 Theorem: (cos x + i sin x)^n = cos nx + i sin nxNot to be confused with [De Moivre–Laplace theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre%E2%80%93Laplace_theorem).

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), **de Moivre's formula** (also known as **de Moivre's theorem** and **de Moivre's identity**) states that for any [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) x and [integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) n,       (   cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x    )    n   = cos ⁡ n x + i sin ⁡ n x ,   {\displaystyle {\big (}\cos x+i\sin x{\big )}^{n}=\cos nx+i\sin nx,}   where i is the [imaginary unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_unit) (*i*2 = −1). The formula is named after [Abraham de Moivre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_de_Moivre),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre's_formula#cite_note-1) although he never stated it in his works.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre's_formula#cite_note-2) The expression cos *x* + *i* sin *x* is sometimes abbreviated to [cis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cis_(mathematics)) *x*.

The formula is important because it connects [complex numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_numbers) and [trigonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometry). By expanding the left hand side and then comparing the real and imaginary parts under the assumption that x is real, it is possible to derive useful expressions for cos *nx* and sin *nx* in terms of cos *x* and sin *x*.

As written, the formula is not valid for non-integer powers n. However, there are generalizations of this formula valid for other exponents. These can be used to give explicit expressions for the nth [roots of unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_unity), that is, [complex numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_numbers) z such that *zn* = 1.

Using the standard extensions of the sine and cosine functions to complex numbers, the formula is valid even when x is an arbitrary complex number.

Example

# Example

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=1)]

For     x =   π 6     {\displaystyle x={\frac {\pi }{6}}}   and     n = 2   {\displaystyle n=2}  , de Moivre's formula asserts that       (  cos ⁡   (     π 6     )   + i sin ⁡   (     π 6     )    )   2   = cos ⁡   (   2 ⋅   π 6     )   + i sin ⁡   (   2 ⋅   π 6     )   ,   {\displaystyle \left(\cos {\bigg (}{\frac {\pi }{6}}{\bigg )}+i\sin {\bigg (}{\frac {\pi }{6}}{\bigg )}\right)^{2}=\cos {\bigg (}2\cdot {\frac {\pi }{6}}{\bigg )}+i\sin {\bigg (}2\cdot {\frac {\pi }{6}}{\bigg )},}   or equivalently that       (     3  2   +   i 2    )   2   =   1 2   +    i   3    2   .   {\displaystyle \left({\frac {\sqrt {3}}{2}}+{\frac {i}{2}}\right)^{2}={\frac {1}{2}}+{\frac {i{\sqrt {3}}}{2}}.}   In this example, it is easy to check the validity of the equation by multiplying out the left side.

Relation to Euler's formula

# Relation to Euler's formula

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=2)]

De Moivre's formula is a precursor to [Euler's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler's_formula)      e  i x   = cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x ,   {\displaystyle e^{ix}=\cos x+i\sin x,}   with x expressed in [radians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radian) rather than [degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_(angle)), which establishes the fundamental relationship between the trigonometric functions and the complex exponential function.

One can derive de Moivre's formula using Euler's formula and the [exponential law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiation) for integer powers

       (  e  i x   )   n   =  e  i n x   ,   {\displaystyle \left(e^{ix}\right)^{n}=e^{inx},}

since Euler's formula implies that the left side is equal to       (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   n     {\displaystyle \left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{n}}   while the right side is equal to     cos ⁡ n x + i sin ⁡ n x .   {\displaystyle \cos nx+i\sin nx.}

Proof by induction

# Proof by induction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=3)]

The truth of de Moivre's theorem can be established by using mathematical induction for natural numbers, and extended to all integers from there. For an integer n, call the following statement S(*n*):

     ( cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )  n   = cos ⁡ n x + i sin ⁡ n x .   {\displaystyle (\cos x+i\sin x)^{n}=\cos nx+i\sin nx.}

For *n* > 0, we proceed by [mathematical induction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_induction). S(1) is clearly true. For our hypothesis, we assume S(*k*) is true for some natural k. That is, we assume

       (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   k   = cos ⁡ k x + i sin ⁡ k x .   {\displaystyle \left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{k}=\cos kx+i\sin kx.}

Now, considering S(*k* + 1):

           (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   k + 1      =   (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   k    (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )        =  (  cos ⁡ k x + i sin ⁡ k x  )   (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )       via induction hypothesis        = cos ⁡ k x cos ⁡ x − sin ⁡ k x sin ⁡ x + i  (  cos ⁡ k x sin ⁡ x + sin ⁡ k x cos ⁡ x  )        = cos ⁡ ( ( k + 1 ) x ) + i sin ⁡ ( ( k + 1 ) x )      via trigonometric identities        {\displaystyle {\begin{alignedat}{2}\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{k+1}&=\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{k}\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)\\&=\left(\cos kx+i\sin kx\right)\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)&&\qquad {\text{via induction hypothesis}}\\&=\cos kx\cos x-\sin kx\sin x+i\left(\cos kx\sin x+\sin kx\cos x\right)\\&=\cos((k+1)x)+i\sin((k+1)x)&&\qquad {\text{via trigonometric identities}}\end{alignedat}}}

See [angle sum and difference identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_identities#Angle_sum_and_difference_identities).

We deduce that S(*k*) implies S(*k* + 1). By the principle of mathematical induction it follows that the result is true for all natural numbers. Now, S(0) is clearly true since cos(0*x*) + *i* sin(0*x*) = 1 + 0*i* = 1. Finally, for the negative integer cases, we consider an exponent of −*n* for natural n.

           (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   − n      =   (     (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   n      )    − 1         =   (  cos ⁡ n x + i sin ⁡ n x  )   − 1         = cos ⁡ n x − i sin ⁡ n x   ( ∗ )       = cos ⁡ ( − n x ) + i sin ⁡ ( − n x ) .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{-n}&={\big (}\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{n}{\big )}^{-1}\\&=\left(\cos nx+i\sin nx\right)^{-1}\\&=\cos nx-i\sin nx\qquad \qquad (*)\\&=\cos(-nx)+i\sin(-nx).\\\end{aligned}}}

The equation (*) is a result of the identity

      z  − 1   =     z ¯     |  z   |   2      ,   {\displaystyle z^{-1}={\frac {\bar {z}}{|z|^{2}}},}

for *z* = cos *nx* + *i* sin *nx*. Hence, S(*n*) holds for all integers n.

Formulae for cosine and sine individually

# Formulae for cosine and sine individually

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=4)] See also: [List of trigonometric identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_trigonometric_identities)

For an equality of [complex numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number), one necessarily has equality both of the [real parts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_part) and of the [imaginary parts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_part) of both members of the equation. If x, and therefore also cos *x* and sin *x*, are [real numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number), then the identity of these parts can be written using [binomial coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_coefficient). This formula was given by 16th century French mathematician [François Viète](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Vi%C3%A8te):

         sin ⁡ n x    =  ∑  k = 0   n      (   n k   )    ( cos ⁡ x  )  k    ( sin ⁡ x  )  n − k    sin ⁡    ( n − k ) π  2       cos ⁡ n x    =  ∑  k = 0   n      (   n k   )    ( cos ⁡ x  )  k    ( sin ⁡ x  )  n − k    cos ⁡    ( n − k ) π  2   .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}\sin nx&=\sum _{k=0}^{n}{\binom {n}{k}}(\cos x)^{k}\,(\sin x)^{n-k}\,\sin {\frac {(n-k)\pi }{2}}\\\cos nx&=\sum _{k=0}^{n}{\binom {n}{k}}(\cos x)^{k}\,(\sin x)^{n-k}\,\cos {\frac {(n-k)\pi }{2}}.\end{aligned}}}

In each of these two equations, the final [trigonometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions) equals one or minus one or zero, thus removing half the entries in each of the sums. These equations are in fact valid even for complex values of x, because both sides are [entire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entire_function) (that is, [holomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holomorphic_function) on the whole [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane)) functions of x, and two such functions that coincide on the real axis necessarily coincide everywhere. Here are the concrete instances of these equations for *n* = 2 and *n* = 3:

         cos ⁡ 2 x    =   (  cos ⁡ x  )   2   +  (    (  cos ⁡ x  )   2   − 1  )      =     2   (  cos ⁡ x  )   2   − 1     sin ⁡ 2 x    = 2  (  sin ⁡ x  )   (  cos ⁡ x  )        cos ⁡ 3 x    =   (  cos ⁡ x  )   3   + 3 cos ⁡ x  (    (  cos ⁡ x  )   2   − 1  )      =     4   (  cos ⁡ x  )   3   − 3 cos ⁡ x     sin ⁡ 3 x    = 3   (  cos ⁡ x  )   2    (  sin ⁡ x  )  −   (  sin ⁡ x  )   3       =     3 sin ⁡ x − 4   (  sin ⁡ x  )   3   .       {\displaystyle {\begin{alignedat}{2}\cos 2x&=\left(\cos x\right)^{2}+\left(\left(\cos x\right)^{2}-1\right)&{}={}&2\left(\cos x\right)^{2}-1\\\sin 2x&=2\left(\sin x\right)\left(\cos x\right)&&\\\cos 3x&=\left(\cos x\right)^{3}+3\cos x\left(\left(\cos x\right)^{2}-1\right)&{}={}&4\left(\cos x\right)^{3}-3\cos x\\\sin 3x&=3\left(\cos x\right)^{2}\left(\sin x\right)-\left(\sin x\right)^{3}&{}={}&3\sin x-4\left(\sin x\right)^{3}.\end{alignedat}}}

The right-hand side of the formula for cos *nx* is in fact the value *T**n*(cos *x*) of the [Chebyshev polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_polynomial) *T**n* at cos *x*.

Failure for non-integer powers, and generalization

# Failure for non-integer powers, and generalization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=5)]

De Moivre's formula does not hold for non-integer powers. The derivation of de Moivre's formula above involves a complex number raised to the integer power n. If a complex number is raised to a non-integer power, the result is [multiple-valued](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple-valued) (see [failure of power and logarithm identities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiation#Failure_of_power_and_logarithm_identities)).

Roots of complex numbers

# Roots of complex numbers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=6)]

A modest extension of the version of de Moivre's formula given in this article can be used to find [the n-th roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nth_root) of a complex number for a non-zero integer n. If z is a complex number, written in [polar form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_form) as     z = r  (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )  ,   {\displaystyle z=r\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right),}   then the n-th roots of z are given by      r   1 n     (  cos ⁡    x + 2 π k  n   + i sin ⁡    x + 2 π k  n    )    {\displaystyle r^{\frac {1}{n}}\left(\cos {\frac {x+2\pi k}{n}}+i\sin {\frac {x+2\pi k}{n}}\right)}   where k varies over the integer values from 0 to |*n*| − 1. This formula is also sometimes known as de Moivre's formula.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre's_formula#cite_note-3)

Complex numbers raised to an arbitrary power

# Complex numbers raised to an arbitrary power

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=7)]

Generally, if     z = r  (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )    {\displaystyle z=r\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)}   (in polar form) and w are arbitrary complex numbers, then the set of possible values is      z  w   =  r  w     (  cos ⁡ x + i sin ⁡ x  )   w   = {  r  w   cos ⁡ ( x w + 2 π k w ) + i  r  w   sin ⁡ ( x w + 2 π k w )  |  k ∈  Z  }  .   {\displaystyle z^{w}=r^{w}\left(\cos x+i\sin x\right)^{w}=\lbrace r^{w}\cos(xw+2\pi kw)+ir^{w}\sin(xw+2\pi kw)|k\in \mathbb {Z} \rbrace \,.}   (Note that if w is a [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number) that equals *p* / *q* in [lowest terms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowest_terms) then this set will have exactly q distinct values rather than infinitely many. In particular, if w is an integer then the set will have exactly one value, as previously discussed.) In contrast, de Moivre's formula gives      r  w   ( cos ⁡ x w + i sin ⁡ x w )  ,   {\displaystyle r^{w}(\cos xw+i\sin xw)\,,}   which is just the single value from this set corresponding to *k* = 0.

Analogues in other settings

# Analogues in other settings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=8)]

Hyperbolic trigonometry

# Hyperbolic trigonometry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=9)]

Since cosh *x* + sinh *x* = *ex*, an analog to de Moivre's formula also applies to the [hyperbolic trigonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_function). For all [integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer) n,

 **( cosh ⁡ x + sinh ⁡ x  )  n   = cosh ⁡ n x + sinh ⁡ n x .   {\displaystyle (\cosh x+\sinh x)^{n}=\cosh nx+\sinh nx.}**

If n is a [rational number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_number) (but not necessarily an integer), then cosh *nx* + sinh *nx* will be one of the values of (cosh *x* + sinh *x*)*n*.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre's_formula#cite_note-4)

Extension to complex numbers

# Extension to complex numbers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=10)]

For any integer n, the formula holds for any complex number     z = x + i y   {\displaystyle z=x+iy}

     ( cos ⁡ z + i sin ⁡ z  )  n   = cos ⁡  n z  + i sin ⁡  n z  .   {\displaystyle (\cos z+i\sin z)^{n}=\cos {nz}+i\sin {nz}.}

where

         cos ⁡ z = cos ⁡ ( x + i y )    = cos ⁡ x cosh ⁡ y − i sin ⁡ x sinh ⁡ y  ,     sin ⁡ z = sin ⁡ ( x + i y )    = sin ⁡ x cosh ⁡ y + i cos ⁡ x sinh ⁡ y  .       {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}\cos z=\cos(x+iy)&=\cos x\cosh y-i\sin x\sinh y\,,\\\sin z=\sin(x+iy)&=\sin x\cosh y+i\cos x\sinh y\,.\end{aligned}}}

Quaternions

# Quaternions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=11)]

To find the roots of a [quaternion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternion) there is an analogous form of de Moivre's formula. A quaternion in the form

     q = d + a    i ^    + b    j ^    + c    k ^      {\displaystyle q=d+a\mathbf {\hat {i}} +b\mathbf {\hat {j}} +c\mathbf {\hat {k}} }

can be represented in the form

     q = k ( cos ⁡ θ + ε sin ⁡ θ )    for    0 ≤ θ < 2 π .   {\displaystyle q=k(\cos \theta +\varepsilon \sin \theta )\qquad {\mbox{for }}0\leq \theta <2\pi .}

In this representation,

     k =    d  2   +  a  2   +  b  2   +  c  2     ,   {\displaystyle k={\sqrt {d^{2}+a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}},}

and the trigonometric functions are defined as

     cos ⁡ θ =   d k      and    sin ⁡ θ = ±     a  2   +  b  2   +  c  2    k   .   {\displaystyle \cos \theta ={\frac {d}{k}}\quad {\mbox{and}}\quad \sin \theta =\pm {\frac {\sqrt {a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}{k}}.}

In the case that *a*2 + *b*2 + *c*2 ≠ 0,

     ε = ±    a    i ^    + b    j ^    + c    k ^       a  2   +  b  2   +  c  2      ,   {\displaystyle \varepsilon =\pm {\frac {a\mathbf {\hat {i}} +b\mathbf {\hat {j}} +c\mathbf {\hat {k}} }{\sqrt {a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}},}

that is, the [unit vector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_vector). This leads to the variation of De Moivre's formula:

      q  n   =  k  n   ( cos ⁡ n θ + ε sin ⁡ n θ ) .   {\displaystyle q^{n}=k^{n}(\cos n\theta +\varepsilon \sin n\theta ).}  [[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Moivre's_formula#cite_note-5)

#### Example

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=12)]

To find the [cube roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cube_root) of

     Q = 1 +    i ^    +    j ^    +    k ^    ,   {\displaystyle Q=1+\mathbf {\hat {i}} +\mathbf {\hat {j}} +\mathbf {\hat {k}} ,}

write the quaternion in the form

     Q = 2  (  cos ⁡   π 3   + ε sin ⁡   π 3    )     where    ε =       i ^    +    j ^    +    k ^      3    .   {\displaystyle Q=2\left(\cos {\frac {\pi }{3}}+\varepsilon \sin {\frac {\pi }{3}}\right)\qquad {\mbox{where }}\varepsilon ={\frac {\mathbf {\hat {i}} +\mathbf {\hat {j}} +\mathbf {\hat {k}} }{\sqrt {3}}}.}

Then the cube roots are given by:

       Q  3    =   2  3    ( cos ⁡ θ + ε sin ⁡ θ )    for    θ =   π 9   ,    7 π  9   ,    13 π  9   .   {\displaystyle {\sqrt[{3}]{Q}}={\sqrt[{3}]{2}}(\cos \theta +\varepsilon \sin \theta )\qquad {\mbox{for }}\theta ={\frac {\pi }{9}},{\frac {7\pi }{9}},{\frac {13\pi }{9}}.}

2 × 2 matrices

# 2 × 2 matrices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=De_Moivre%27s_formula&action=edit&section=13)]

With matrices,        (    cos ⁡ ϕ   − sin ⁡ ϕ     sin ⁡ ϕ   cos ⁡ ϕ    )    n   =   (    cos ⁡ n ϕ   − sin ⁡ n ϕ     sin ⁡ n ϕ   cos ⁡ n ϕ    )     {\displaystyle {\begin{pmatrix}\cos \phi &-\sin \phi \\\sin \phi &\cos \phi \end{pmatrix}}^{n}={\begin{pmatrix}\cos n\phi &-\sin n\phi \\\sin n\phi &\cos n\phi \end{pmatrix}}}   when n is an integer. This is a direct consequence of the [isomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphism) between the matrices of type       (    a   − b     b   a    )     {\displaystyle {\begin{pmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{pmatrix}}}   and the [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane).
